title: Tracking Global Ocean Heat
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Oceans cover seventy percent of the Earth and store vast amounts of energy. This stored energy is known as ocean heat content. It serves as an important indicator of global warming and helps scientists understand our changing climate and environmental stability over time.
pages.caption: The ocean heat content (OHC) has been increasing for decades as the ocean has been absorbing most of the excess heat resulting from greenhouse gas emissions from human activities. The graph shows OHC calculated to a water depth of 700 and 2000 meters.

evidence.articleCaption: The ocean heat content (OHC) has been increasing for decades as the ocean has been absorbing most of the excess heat resulting from greenhouse gas emissions from human activities. The graph shows OHC calculated to a water depth of 700 and 2000 meters.

pages.text: Between 1971 and 2018, oceans took in over ninety percent of the extra energy from global warming. Human greenhouse gas emissions are the main reason for this change.
pages.caption: Chart of different thermoclines (depth versus ocean temperature) based on seasons and latitude

evidence.articleCaption: Chart of different thermoclines (depth versus ocean temperature) based on seasons and latitude

pages.text: Scientists measure ocean temperatures at many different locations and depths. Since the year 2000, an expanding network of nearly four thousand robotic Argo floats has helped measure temperature anomalies and changes in ocean heat all around the world.
pages.caption: The global distribution of active floats in the Argo array

evidence.fileTitle: File:Argo floats in Feb. 2018 colour coded by country.png
evidence.articleCaption: The global distribution of active floats in the Argo array

pages.text: Changes in ocean temperature greatly affect ecosystems in oceans and on land. Warming water affects marine life and causes variations in sea level and sea ice. It also changes the intensity of the water cycle and the migration of marine species.
pages.caption: Earth heat inventory (energy accumulation) in ZJ for the components of the Earth's climate system relative to 1960 and from 1960 to 2018. The upper ocean (0–300 m, light blue line, and 0–700 m, light blue shading) accounts for the largest amount of heat gain.

evidence.articleCaption: Earth heat inventory (energy accumulation) in ZJ for the components of the Earth's climate system relative to 1960 and from 1960 to 2018. The upper ocean (0–300 m, light blue line, and 0–700 m, light blue shading) accounts for the largest amount of heat gain.

pages.text: Between 1971 and 2018, a steady upward trend in ocean heat content accounted for over ninety percent of Earth's excess energy from global warming. Increased ocean heat in response to anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions is essentially irreversible on human time scales.

Ocean heat content measures the energy absorbed and stored by the world's oceans. Because oceans cover seventy percent of the Earth and have a high heat capacity, they play a critical role in climate stability.

pages.text: Since 1971, a steady upward trend in ocean heat has accounted for over ninety percent of Earth's excess energy from global warming. This trend is driven primarily by human-caused greenhouse gas emissions that trap planetary heat.

pages.text: Warming oceans drive sea level rise, coral bleaching, and the migration of marine species. Monitoring ocean heat content remains essential for accurate climate models and understanding long-term trends.

C1-C2.headline: The Dynamics of Ocean Heat Uptake

pages.text: Ocean heat content quantifies the thermodynamic potential energy stored within seawater basins. Because oceans possess a high heat capacity and cover seventy percent of the planetary surface, they absorb the vast majority of excess anthropogenic heat.
pages.caption: The ocean heat content (OHC) has been increasing for decades as the ocean has been absorbing most of the excess heat resulting from greenhouse gas emissions from human activities. The graph shows OHC calculated to a water depth of 700 and 2000 meters.

evidence.articleCaption: The ocean heat content (OHC) has been increasing for decades as the ocean has been absorbing most of the excess heat resulting from greenhouse gas emissions from human activities. The graph shows OHC calculated to a water depth of 700 and 2000 meters.

pages.text: Observational data reveals a robust multi-decadal upward trajectory, with ocean heat uptake accounting for over ninety percent of Earth's net energy imbalance since 1971. This persistent warming is fundamentally driven by rising atmospheric greenhouse gases.
pages.caption: Chart of different thermoclines (depth versus ocean temperature) based on seasons and latitude

pages.text: Historical assessments relied on research vessels and stations, whereas contemporary monitoring utilizes approximately four thousand robotic profiling floats deployed through the international Argo program to measure subsurface temperature anomalies and track regional variations in heat uptake.

pages.text: Regional variations in heat uptake are pronounced. The extratropical Southern Ocean has absorbed a disproportionate share of thermal energy, contributing to regional sea ice reduction and influencing global overturning circulation.
pages.caption: Earth heat inventory (energy accumulation) in ZJ for the components of the Earth's climate system relative to 1960 and from 1960 to 2018. The upper ocean (0–300 m, light blue line, and 0–700 m, light blue shading) accounts for the largest amount of heat gain.

pages.text: The resulting thermal expansion drives ongoing sea level rise and triggers ecological disruptions such as coral bleaching. Due to the immense thermal inertia of the oceans, these increases remain virtually irreversible on human time scales.

title: Exploring the History and Geography of Hadhramaut
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Hadhramaut is a large region in the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula. Its lands stretch from a big desert in the north down to the sea. The people who live there are known as the Hadharem. They speak their own dialect of Arabic today.
pages.caption: An ancient sculpture of a griffin, from the royal palace at Shabwa, the then-capital city of Hadhramaut

evidence.fileTitle: File:Decorated capital from the Royal Palace of Shabwat.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: An ancient sculpture of a griffin, from the royal palace at Shabwa, the then-capital city of Hadhramaut

pages.text: People have different ideas about where the name Hadhramaut comes from. One popular story says it means death has come. Another idea connects it to an old biblical name. Long ago, people in the area made things from stone and lived in caves.
pages.caption: The ruins of Sumhuram in Khor Rori

evidence.articleCaption: The ruins of Sumhuram in Khor Rori

pages.text: In ancient times, a kingdom was built here with its capital at Shabwa. The early wealth of this region came from the trade of valuable incense. Caravans traveled along desert routes, and rulers taxed them for protection along the way.
pages.caption: The flag of Hadhramaut in the Battle of Siffin

evidence.articleCaption: The flag of Hadhramaut in the Battle of Siffin

pages.text: Islam reached the region in the seventh century after a messenger was sent by the prophet Muhammad. Later, different groups and sultanates controlled the land. In the sixteenth century, the Portuguese arrived on the coast but were driven out.
pages.caption: Hadhramaut in a 1732 copy of the map by Ottoman geographer Kâtip Çelebi (1609–57), from the first printed atlas in the Ottoman Empire

evidence.fileTitle: File:Hadhramaut in Houghton Typ 794.34.475 - Kâtip Çelebi, Kitab-ı cihannüma (cropped).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Hadhramaut in a 1732 copy of the map by Ottoman geographer Kâtip Çelebi (1609–57), from the first printed atlas in the Ottoman Empire

pages.text: Today, the region includes major cities like Mukalla and Tarim. People farm dates and grains in the green river valleys. Fishing along the long coast also provides food and jobs for many local families living near the sea.

B1-B2.headline: Exploring the History and Geography of Hadhramaut

pages.text: Hadhramaut is a geographic region in the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula, encompassing parts of modern Yemen, Oman, and Saudi Arabia. Its physical landscape divides clearly into Inner Hadhramaut around the main wadi, a coastal plain, and a high plateau sloping northward into the desert.
pages.caption: An ancient sculpture of a griffin, from the royal palace at Shabwa, the then-capital city of Hadhramaut

evidence.fileTitle: File:Decorated capital from the Royal Palace of Shabwat.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: An ancient sculpture of a griffin, from the royal palace at Shabwa, the then-capital city of Hadhramaut

pages.text: The exact origins of the name remain disputed, with several debated hypotheses. Traditional folk explanations connect the word to a legendary settler whose nickname meant death has come, while other traditions link the name to ancient biblical references and early prophets of the region.
pages.caption: The ruins of Sumhuram in Khor Rori

evidence.articleCaption: The ruins of Sumhuram in Khor Rori

pages.text: Human activity in the area dates back to the Middle Palaeolithic, followed by prehistoric megalithic structures and stone circles. By the early first millennium BCE, the organized Kingdom of Hadhramaut emerged, gaining independence and growing prosperous through its vital role in the ancient incense trade.
pages.caption: The flag of Hadhramaut in the Battle of Siffin

evidence.articleCaption: The flag of Hadhramaut in the Battle of Siffin

pages.text: Islam arrived in the region around 630 following a message from the prophet Muhammad, though local tribes initially resisted. Over the following centuries, various sultanates and foreign powers, including Portuguese traders and Ottoman administrators, exerted control over different parts of the territory.
pages.caption: Hadhramaut in a 1732 copy of the map by Ottoman geographer Kâtip Çelebi (1609–57), from the first printed atlas in the Ottoman Empire

pages.text: By the twentieth century, returning emigrants funded modernization projects like motor roads, though these plans faced resistance from local camel owners. Following periods of political transition and communist rule, Hadhramaut is now known for port cities like Mukalla, traditional farming, and coastal fishing.

Hadhramaut constitutes a distinct geographic expanse within the southern Arabian Peninsula, traditionally incorporating territories across modern Yemen, Oman, and Saudi Arabia. Topographically, the region transitions from the hyper-arid expanse of the Empty Quarter through the fertile Wadi Hadhramaut down to a narrow coastal plain bounded by a steep escarpment.

pages.text: Etymological derivations for the toponym remain contested, with multiple competing hypotheses persisting. Popular folk etymologies attribute the name to a legendary progenitor signifying death has come, whereas alternative scholarly and traditional perspectives align the terminology with ancient Semitic roots and biblical nomenclature.
pages.caption: The ruins of Sumhuram in Khor Rori

evidence.articleCaption: The ruins of Sumhuram in Khor Rori

pages.text: Archaeological evidence indicates human habitation extending from the Middle Palaeolithic, succeeded by megalithic monuments. By the early first millennium BCE, the centralized Kingdom of Hadhramaut consolidated power, capitalizing strategically on the lucrative overland incense trade routes until maritime route shifts redirected economic dynamics.
pages.caption: The flag of Hadhramaut in the Battle of Siffin

evidence.articleCaption: The flag of Hadhramaut in the Battle of Siffin

pages.text: Islamic integration commenced circa 630 CE through emissaries dispatched by Muhammad, encountering substantial resistance from indigenous populations and traditional aristocracies. Subsequent centuries witnessed fluctuating governance under regional sultanates, alongside temporary incursions by Portuguese naval forces and long-term Ottoman administrative influence.
pages.caption: Hadhramaut in a 1732 copy of the map by Ottoman geographer Kâtip Çelebi (1609–57), from the first printed atlas in the Ottoman Empire

pages.text: Twentieth-century modernization efforts, financed largely by affluent expatriate families, frequently engendered socioeconomic friction with traditional transport guilds. Following complex mid-century political realignments and integration into the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen, the region currently sustains its economy through localized agriculture, maritime fisheries, and urban trade centers like Mukalla.

title: History of the Silk Road
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The Silk Road was not a single path. It was a big network of trade routes connecting Asia, Africa, and Europe. People used these routes for a very long time, from the second century BCE until the mid-fifteenth century.
pages.caption: Woven silk textile from Tomb No. 1 at Mawangdui, Changsha, Hunan province, China, dated to the Western Han Era, 2nd century BCE

evidence.articleCaption: Woven silk textile from Tomb No. 1 at Mawangdui, Changsha, Hunan province, China, dated to the Western Han Era, 2nd century BCE

pages.text: The name came from the trade in silk, which was made in China. The Han dynasty helped start this network when they moved into Central Asia. China built parts of the Great Wall to keep the trade routes safe.
pages.caption: Main routes of the Silk Road on a relief map, with city and region names labeled

evidence.articleCaption: Main routes of the Silk Road on a relief map, with city and region names labeled

pages.text: Many things traveled along these roads. China sent silk, tea, and porcelain. The West sent horses, gold, and camels. People also shared religious and scientific ideas as they traveled from place to place along the paths.
pages.caption: The Silk Road in the 1st century

evidence.fileTitle: File:Silk Road in the I century AD - en.svg
evidence.articleCaption: The Silk Road in the 1st century

pages.text: Traveling was hard and dangerous because there were bandits and very difficult land. Most people did not travel the whole way. Instead, local middlemen helped move goods from one stopping point to the next.
pages.caption: Chinese jade and steatite plaques, in the Scythian-style animal art of the steppes. 4th–3rd century BCE. British Museum.

pages.text: Later, the Ottoman Empire competed for control over these land routes. This made European countries look for new ways to trade, which started the Age of Discovery and changed world history.

The Silk Road was an extensive network of trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century. Spanning thousands of kilometers on land and sea, it connected the Eastern and Western worlds, facilitating economic, cultural, and religious interactions between diverse civilizations.
pages.caption: Woven silk textile from Tomb No. 1 at Mawangdui, Changsha, Hunan province, China, dated to the Western Han Era, 2nd century BCE

evidence.articleCaption: Woven silk textile from Tomb No. 1 at Mawangdui, Changsha, Hunan province, China, dated to the Western Han Era, 2nd century BCE

pages.text: The name derives from the lucrative trade of silk textiles produced primarily in China. The network expanded when the Han dynasty moved into Central Asia. To protect these valuable trade products, the Chinese extended the Great Wall and relied on partners like the Parthian Empire as a bridge to the Mediterranean.
pages.caption: Main routes of the Silk Road on a relief map, with city and region names labeled

evidence.articleCaption: Main routes of the Silk Road on a relief map, with city and region names labeled

pages.text: By the first century CE, Chinese silk was highly sought after in Rome, Egypt, and Greece. Other major Eastern exports included tea, dyes, perfumes, and porcelain, while Western traders provided horses, camels, honey, wine, and gold, generating substantial wealth for mercantile classes.
pages.caption: The Silk Road in the 1st century

evidence.fileTitle: File:Silk Road in the I century AD - en.svg
evidence.articleCaption: The Silk Road in the 1st century

pages.text: The network was highly decentralized and lacked heavy security, exposing travelers to constant threats of banditry, nomadic raiders, and harsh terrain. Few individuals traversed the entire length, choosing instead to rely on a succession of middlemen at various stopping points.
pages.caption: Chinese jade and steatite plaques, in the Scythian-style animal art of the steppes. 4th–3rd century BCE. British Museum.

imageProvenance.credit: No machine-readable author provided. World Imaging assumed (based on copyright claims).

evidence.articleCaption: Chinese jade and steatite plaques, in the Scythian-style animal art of the steppes. 4th–3rd century BCE. British Museum.

pages.text: Beyond commercial goods, the routes enabled an unprecedented exchange of religious, philosophical, and scientific thought, alongside the spread of diseases. In the 15th century, Ottoman competition over the routes encouraged European nations to seek alternative paths, leading to the Age of Discovery.

The Silk Road comprised an intricate transcontinental web of land and sea routes operating from the second century BCE through the mid-15th century. Rather than a singular east-west corridor, it connected Central, East, South, Southeast, and West Asia, alongside East Africa and Southern Europe, fundamentally shaping interregional relations.
pages.caption: Woven silk textile from Tomb No. 1 at Mawangdui, Changsha, Hunan province, China, dated to the Western Han Era, 2nd century BCE

evidence.articleCaption: Woven silk textile from Tomb No. 1 at Mawangdui, Changsha, Hunan province, China, dated to the Western Han Era, 2nd century BCE

pages.text: Etymologically linked to the lucrative commerce in Chinese silk textiles, the network formalized with the Han dynasty's 2nd-century BCE expansion into Central Asia under Emperor Wu and envoy Zhang Qian. Strategic security measures, including extensions of the Great Wall and diplomatic bridges provided by the Parthian Empire, integrated the system toward the Mediterranean.
pages.caption: Main routes of the Silk Road on a relief map, with city and region names labeled

evidence.articleCaption: Main routes of the Silk Road on a relief map, with city and region names labeled

pages.text: By the first century CE, demand for Chinese silk flourished across Rome, Greece, and Egypt. Alongside commodities like tea, porcelain, and spices, Western exports such as gold, horses, and camels traversed the system, empowering emerging mercantile classes and disseminating transformative technologies like paper and gunpowder.
pages.caption: The Silk Road in the 1st century

evidence.fileTitle: File:Silk Road in the I century AD - en.svg
evidence.articleCaption: The Silk Road in the 1st century

pages.text: Characterized by decentralization and sparse security, the routes exposed travelers to severe terrain, banditry, and nomadic raiders. Consequently, traversal of the entire network was rare; merchants instead relied on decentralized networks of middlemen stationed at successive regional hubs along the way.

pages.text: Crucially, the infrastructure functioned as a conduit for intellectual, scientific, and religious transmission—particularly Buddhism—while inadvertently facilitating epidemiological vectors such as plague. The subsequent rise of the Ottoman Empire disrupted overland transit, compelling European polities to pioneer maritime alternatives during the Age of Discovery.

The Silk Road was an extensive network of trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century. Spanning thousands of kilometers on land and sea, it connected the Eastern and Western worlds, facilitating economic, cultural, and religious interactions between diverse civilizations.

pages.text: The name derives from the lucrative trade of silk textiles produced primarily in China. The network expanded when the Han dynasty moved into Central Asia. To protect these valuable trade products, the Chinese extended the Great Wall and relied on partners like the Parthian Empire as a bridge to the Mediterranean.

pages.text: By the first century CE, Chinese silk was highly sought after in Rome, Egypt, and Greece. Other major Eastern exports included tea, dyes, perfumes, and porcelain, while Western traders provided horses, camels, honey, wine, and gold, generating substantial wealth for mercantile classes.

pages.text: The network was highly decentralized and lacked heavy security, exposing travelers to constant threats of banditry, nomadic raiders, and harsh terrain. Few individuals traversed the entire length, choosing instead to rely on a succession of middlemen at various stopping points.

pages.text: Beyond commercial goods, the routes enabled an unprecedented exchange of religious, philosophical, and scientific thought, alongside the spread of diseases. In the 15th century, Ottoman competition over the routes encouraged European nations to seek alternative paths, leading to the Age of Discovery.
